summary: Provides an architectural description and concept of operations for some optional, advanced deployment scenarios for the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP). None of them is required for using ILNP. It is an experimental document.

eli5.summary: These are extra ideas, like optional toppings, for how people might use ILNP, which separates a computer's name from its address. None of the toppings are needed.

subtitle: Advanced optional deployment patterns for networks using identifier-locator separation.

tldr.problem: The Identifier-Locator Network Protocol separates names from addresses, but administrators need guidance on how to use this architecture in real deployments involving multihoming, mobility, and local addressing.
tldr.mechanism: This document provides architectural patterns and operational concepts for ILNP deployment in scenarios like site multihoming, network mobility, traffic engineering, datacentres, and privacy protection.
tldr.outcome: The document is experimental and describes optional capabilities; none are required for basic ILNP use. It remains a research document without standards-track status.

facts.label: Core concept
facts.value: Site Border Router manages locator rewriting

today: RFC 6748 is experimental and not on the standards track. It remains a research document describing optional ILNP deployment patterns that are not required for basic ILNP operation.

sections.title: Advanced ILNP Deployment Options
sections.content:
ILNP is an experimental evolution of IP that separates identifiers (names) from locators (addresses). While the basic architecture is covered elsewhere, this document describes optional deployment scenarios that use a Site Border Router (SBR) to manage these locator and identifier values for an entire site, rather than requiring each host to do so independently.

These patterns are not required for ILNP to work; they are engineering conveniences for specific deployment needs. The document addresses multihoming, mobility, traffic engineering, virtual machine mobility, and privacy.
sections.eli5: ILNP is like giving everyone in town both a name and a street address. This paper explains clever ways to use that separation for managing networks.

sections.title: Localised Numbering
sections.content:
A Site Border Router can advertise local, private locator values internally (such as IPv6 ULA prefixes) while maintaining global locators externally. The SBR rewrites locators on packets in both directions, converting between the internal representation and the global one. Because ILNP decouples locators from the transport layer checksum, this rewriting is stateless and has low overhead.

The SBR needs a way to map the global locator received in ingress packets back to the correct internal subnet. If the internal network has subnets, the SBR can manage a simple lookup table for subnet selectors, allowing flexible topology hiding without burdening the site administrator with complex configurations.
sections.eli5: Imagine your house uses private street names, but outside your gate, a router translates them to the real city streets. Packets flow in both directions automatically.

sections.title: Site Multihoming and Mobility
sections.content:
The SBR can manage multihoming for an entire site using the localised numbering mechanism. When a site has multiple upstream links with different locators (from different ISPs), the SBR decides which link to use for outgoing traffic based on policy. If a link fails, the SBR can transparently migrate active sessions to the backup link and notify remote correspondents using Locator Update messages, while internal hosts remain unaware of the change.

Site (network) mobility works similarly: as the entire site moves to a new connection point, the SBR updates its locators and notifies correspondents. The SBR can enable soft-handover during transitions, where both paths are briefly active, reducing packet loss during the move.
sections.eli5: If you move to a new address, the router tells everyone where you are now. They can keep talking to you without knowing you moved.

sections.title: Traffic Engineering and Load Balancing
sections.content:
An SBR can implement sophisticated traffic steering by rewriting locators based on source or destination identifier values and local policy. For example, traffic from one host can be sent via one upstream link while traffic from another goes via a different link, enabling load balancing and service-specific path control. These policies can change dynamically; the SBR migrates affected sessions to new locators by sending Locator Update messages, a process transparent to the hosts themselves.

The mechanism also supports Locator Rewriting Relays (LRRs) for location privacy: packets can be forwarded through a chain of relays that rewrite locators, obscuring the true topological location from observers, similar to onion routing.
sections.eli5: Different types of traffic can take different routes, or shift routes when congestion happens. Nobody at your end needs to know.

sections.title: Datacentre and Privacy Applications
sections.content:
Virtual machine mobility within or between datacentres benefits from ILNP's identity-location separation. If VMs in the same site share the same locator value, moving a VM between physical hosts is purely a local operation; remote correspondents see no change in the packet signatures. For cross-datacentre moves, the SBR can either hide the movement (by routing all traffic through the original SBR) or make it visible (by having the VM announce a new locator and update DNS).

Location privacy is enabled by the Locator Rewriting Relay (LRR) mechanism, which operates outside the realm of cryptographic tunnels, providing lightweight topological anonymity against off-path observers. Identity privacy can also be protected using anonymized identifier values, placing no special burden on the network infrastructure.
sections.eli5: Virtual servers can move between computers without disrupting calls, and you can route through helpers to hide your location.
